crime: By the warden's leave the builder kept the guest-house furnishings in repair, tools and timber stored in the earth-sprite room. In the early weeks the builder set her to the first cuts for a stool; the saw wandered, and board after board came out short. The builder took the cutting back and offered the arrangement that became their standing way: the builder begins, she finishes.
Months of it. Girls left half-done things at her elbow and they came back done; the room called hers the hands that finish anything. She had never begun a single thing.

At dinner the builder announced it before the room, meaning it as a gift: in the morning they would set the finished cabinet in its place, and after that the next piece was hers alone — whole, from the first cut, in front of everyone.

The tall cabinet for the water-sprite room stood all but done that afternoon — eight pegs cut, counted, left to drive. The builder told the helper girl eight remained, asked her to carry the shelf-boards over for the morning, and stayed in company from dinner to the lock.

On her usual evening she crossed to the earth-sprite room; her power completed the cabinet at once — whole and flawless. The helper girl, coming to leave the boards, found her beside the finished piece; the lounge saw the helper come back, and saw her come in later, before the lock.
Alone in between, she drew the two front pegs that pin the body to its base — the pair a mover's tilt bears on — out whole with the pincers from the builder's kit, and pocketed them.

At first light the builder and the helper girl came for the cabinet. The builder walked every finished piece to its place herself. The builder tilted the cabinet toward herself; the body parted from the base at the freed joint and came down on the builder.

Six pegs stood home; of eight cut, two bores at the front of the base stood empty, whole, and clean — no stub, no splinter, no peg anywhere in the room. A split peg leaves its shards and a fallen peg lies where it drops; these were drawn out whole and carried away. The night was locked; from the count to the fall, the one hand at the piece was hers.
fields.epitaph: Hand her a beginning and she was a master; hand her nothing, and she was the slow one again.
fields.epithet: The Hand That Finished Everything and Began Nothing
execution: A frame on the stand held every piece of a simple brace, laid out loose. Not one had been joined.
She bent over the parts. Above her a press was descending toward the frame; a finished brace, set in its housing, would trip the catch that stayed it.
The parts lay untouched. The press came down over her and crushed her against the frame.

magic.name: the Finishing Hand
magic.text: The Finishing Hand — When someone else has started a task and set it aside, her hands can finish it at once — perfectly, and exactly as its beginner intended.
